<a id="entry-bring-the-ontology-kit-source-onto-main"></a>

## Entry 1 — 2026-09-08 — Bring the Ontology Kit source onto main

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

`main` had governance and agent-instruction scaffolding installed (Project Narrative) but no
product code yet; the actual Ontology Kit implementation existed only on a branch whose history no
longer connected to `main`, so a normal PR/merge wasn't possible (GitHub refuses a PR between
branches with no common history).

## Decision

Rather than force-pushing over either branch's history, created a new branch from `main` and
copied the kit's tree onto it file by file, checking each path for a collision first. Only one
file (`README.md`) existed on both sides, and it was already identical, so nothing needed
reconciling by hand.

## Consequences

`main` now contains the full kit: installer, linter, templates, skill, and test suite, alongside
the existing Project Narrative scaffold. `feat/ontology-kit` (the orphaned branch) is left in
place, unmerged, for reference. No shared history exists between it and `main`; future work should
branch from `main` going forward.

<a id="entry-add-codeowners-naming-the-repository-owner"></a>

## Entry 2 — 2026-09-08 — Add CODEOWNERS naming the repository owner

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

`main` had no branch protection and no CODEOWNERS, so any push could land directly with no review.
The repository is moving to a required-review model for `main`.

## Decision

Added a single catch-all CODEOWNERS entry (`* @jamiemitchellconsultants`) rather than per-path
ownership, since there is currently one maintainer. Branch protection (required PR review, required
code-owner review, admin override allowed) is applied separately via the GitHub API/UI, not in this
PR, since it's a repository setting rather than repository content.

## Consequences

Once branch protection is enabled, pull requests into `main` will require review before merging,
except that repository admins can override the requirement. Future maintainers or path-specific
owners can be added to CODEOWNERS by extending this file with more specific patterns above the
catch-all line.

<a id="entry-design-and-plan-owl-ttl-machine-readable-ontology"></a>

## Entry 3 — 2026-09-08 — Design and plan: OWL/TTL machine-readable ontology

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The kit's ontology was Markdown-only: easy for humans and agents to read and diff, but nothing
about it was machine-readable, and it was hand-maintained — exactly the two-representations-drift
problem the rest of the kit exists to close for domain vocabulary generally.

## Decision

`ontology.ttl` becomes the authoritative file; `ontology.md` becomes generated output, regenerated
by a new `build-ontology.mjs` (migrate once if no `.ttl` exists, then always render), enforced by a
new CI staleness check. A small kit-owned OWL vocabulary (`kit:` namespace) gives every ontology
section a formal type. Considered and rejected: hand-maintaining both files with a drift check
instead of generation (more flexible, but drift-prone); shipping Narrative's own files as kit
templates (rejected — Narrative is a separate tool this kit doesn't own, so the spec recommends it
but only scaffolds on explicit agreement, using this repository's own files as the worked example).

## Consequences

Editing the ontology moves from `ontology.md` to `ontology.ttl`; the `.md` becomes a reviewable,
generated artifact, similar to `Narrative.md`. A new `docs/ai-agent-install.md` becomes the primary
onboarding path for an AI agent given a short "add the ontology kit" prompt. The `kit:` vocabulary
is now a design commitment — widening it later is a breaking change to the parser/renderer, not a
docs update. Implementation is not yet started; this PR is spec and plan only.

<a id="entry-implement-owl-ttl-machine-readable-ontology"></a>

## Entry 4 — 2026-09-08 — Implement OWL/TTL machine-readable ontology

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

PR #6 merged the approved spec and implementation plan making `ontology.ttl` the authoritative ontology source with `ontology.md` generated from it. The kit was still Markdown-only: nothing machine-readable, and the `.md` hand-maintained. This PR is the implementation of that plan (all ten tasks), verified by `npm test` (243 pass) plus an end-to-end install-migrate-check run in a scratch repo.

## Decision

Implemented the plan as written, with two corrections discovered during implementation where the plan contradicted itself: (1) `modelToTriples` emits `kit:invariant` triples inline with their concept's class triples rather than in a trailing loop, because subject-grouped Turtle serialization otherwise breaks the specified `parse(serialize(x)) === x` round trip; (2) the plan's entity-triple test expectation was updated to include the invariant annotation the spec mandates on the same subject. Also registered the new `NAMESPACE_URI`/`ONTOLOGY_TTL_PATH` placeholders in `tests/templates.test.mjs` and refreshed README's installed-file list, which the plan left stale. Rejected alternative: weakening the round-trip tests to order-insensitive comparison — kept them exact and fixed the implementation instead.

## Consequences

Adopting repositories edit `ontology.ttl` and regenerate `ontology.md` via `node scripts/build-ontology.mjs`; CI fails on a stale `.md` before the term check runs. The shipped example `ontology.md` lost its section guidance prose (it cannot round-trip through TTL) — that material now lives only in the skill references. The `kit:` vocabulary is now a design commitment: widening it later breaks the parser/renderer pair. `ontology-setup` is a Claude Code skill, so generic agents use the new `docs/ai-agent-install.md` runbook instead.

<a id="entry-chore-dogfood-the-ontology-kit-on-its-own-repository"></a>

## Entry 5 — 2026-09-08 — chore: dogfood the ontology kit on its own repository

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The kit installs a vocabulary discipline into other repositories but had never run it against itself. Its own docs (`README.md`, `docs/how-it-works.md`, the `ontology-setup` skill's reference guides) already carry real domain vocabulary — `Installer`, `TargetRepository`, `OntologyConfig`, `Ownership`, and so on — with no mechanism keeping it from drifting the same way the kit warns adopters it will.

## Decision

Installed the kit into its own repository rather than leaving it undogfooded, and seeded the ontology from the kit's real code and docs rather than filling in the template's placeholder rows. Excluded `templates/` and `docs/superpowers/` from the check via `ignorePaths` instead of trying to make their contents (deliberately generic example terms meant for adopters, and an archived planning transcript full of test fixtures) pass as real domain vocabulary — forcing either into the ontology would have been decoration, not discipline.

## Consequences

This repository is now bound by its own protocol: any future change to the installer, the config shape, or the kit's own vocabulary must update `docs/ontology.md` in the same commit, and CI enforces it via `.github/workflows/ontology-lint.yml`. The allowlist currently holds 14 entries, all illustrative placeholders in reference docs rather than real drift — worth revisiting if that ratio grows as the kit's own documentation expands.

<a id="entry-docs-feature-accept-semantic-ontology-matching-vision"></a>

## Entry 7 — 2026-10-30 — docs(feature): accept semantic ontology matching vision

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The kit's current semantic reviewer is optional, advisory, and examines only added lines. The feature discussion established a different product need: trusted collaborators' PRs should be checked for semantic mismatches across each changed Markdown file, with a path for agents to resolve findings and maintainers to dismiss false positives.

## Decision

Accept the vision in `docs/features/semantic-ontology-matching/01-vision.md`: findings block merge; model or configuration failure is reported as not reviewed and does not block; repository maintainers own model configuration and credentials; the PR author's agent may commit corrections under the author's identity, while other agents propose them; a maintainer may dismiss a specific false positive with a recorded reason. The pilot has no numerical value target and may be disabled if maintainers see no subjective value.

## Consequences

The analyst and architect phases must define the exact review, resolution, and secure execution behavior. This PR records product intent; it does not yet change the existing reviewer or its advisory documentation. Fork PRs remain outside this feature and have a separate manual-investigation issue (#21).

<a id="entry-docs-feature-define-semantic-matching-behaviours"></a>

## Entry 8 — 2026-10-30 — docs(feature): define semantic matching behaviours

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted vision in #14 and PR #22 calls for blocking semantic findings on trusted collaborators' same-repository PRs. The existing optional reviewer is advisory and examines added lines only. The analyst phase had to make the check's observable behavior explicit, including outage, partial review, correction, and dismissal cases.

## Decision

Accept B1–B14 in `docs/features/semantic-ontology-matching/02-behaviours.md`. Review the full current contents of changed eligible Markdown files against the PR's proposed ontology. An active finding blocks merge; the author's agent may correct the branch under the author's identity, while another agent proposes a correction. A maintainer may dismiss a specific finding with a recorded reason for the current revision. The latest run controls the check, so an unavailable or unusable model permits merge with an explicit not-reviewed notice, even after an earlier blocking finding. A partial run blocks if it returned a finding; otherwise it permits merge with incomplete-coverage notice. Repository maintainers control model configuration and credentials. Fork PRs remain outside the automated scope under #21.

## Consequences

The architect must design trusted execution, model configuration, run and dismissal persistence, and PR-visible findings and notices around these behaviors. The outage policy intentionally allows a later failed run to clear an earlier semantic block; the prior finding stays visible as history. The deterministic term check remains independent. This PR introduces behavior and vocabulary only; it does not turn on a semantic check.

Verification: ontology term check passed (60 files, 27 terms); `npm test` passed (243 tests).

<a id="entry-docs-feature-define-semantic-review-architecture"></a>

## Entry 9 — 2026-10-30 — docs(feature): define semantic review architecture

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted behaviours in PR #25 require a semantic finding to block a trusted collaborator's PR, while an unavailable later run permits merge and reports that review did not run. The reviewer needs model credentials, author-supplied Markdown as input, durable findings and dismissals, and a PR status that branch protection can require. The kit's existing advisory reviewer runs from the PR checkout and remains an optional separate path during the pilot.

## Decision

Use a secretless PR trigger followed by trusted default-branch code in a `workflow_run` worker. Read model settings from the default branch's `OntologyConfig` and use a default-branch-only Actions environment secret. Fetch PR contents as data, review all changed eligible Markdown in bounded requests, and validate grounded findings. Publish the latest result in a fixed required commit-status context, keeping each run and each reasoned dismissal visible in PR comments. Ship the blocking path as a separate opt-in so existing advisory installations do not become blocking on upgrade.

## Entry 14 — 2026-11-02 — docs(feature): behaviours for source knowledge graph

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted vision in #42 calls for a source-owned graph that grounds AI agents and can support wider views than the ontology alone. A single repository need not contain every fact needed for all C4 levels. The analyst needed to decide which sources may supply evidence, when a changed file blocks the PR check, and whether inferred relationships can be published.

## Decision

Include selected design and architecture documents as evidence alongside code, tests, ontology terms, and eligible deployment files. A changed file inside declared graph coverage requires a graph refresh or an explicit record that review found no fact change; the deterministic pull-request check blocks when that review is missing. Publish inferred relationships only when they are clearly labeled and cite reviewable source observations, and present them as tentative to agents.

Maintainers can review direct assertions, inferences, evidence, and gaps in the same PR. CI can check structure and freshness but cannot establish semantic truth, so maintainers remain responsible for claims. Repositories can declare partial coverage; out-of-scope files do not trigger the freshness check. <a id="entry-docs-feature-architecture-for-source-knowledge-graph"></a>

## Entry 15 — 2026-11-02 — docs(feature): architecture for source knowledge graph

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted vision and behaviours require source-owned, reviewable facts for AI agent grounding, labeled inferences, explicit gaps, and a blocking PR freshness check within declared coverage. The design must work across C#, TypeScript, Java, and Python, permit selected documents as evidence, use only Terraform for JointBooking deployment evidence, and avoid a required external graph service or Graphify dependency. Adopting repositories already use `ontology.ttl` as the ontology source of truth.

## Decision

Store the graph as canonical Turtle files with named resources and shared ontology concept IRIs. Derive the effective revision from the containing Git commit ([ADR 0005](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/InternalOntology/blob/feature/source-knowledge-graph/architect/docs/adr/0005-source-graph-git-data.md)). Record reviewed source blob IDs and check changed paths against both base and proposed coverage ([ADR 0006](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/InternalOntology/blob/feature/source-knowledge-graph/architect/docs/adr/0006-source-graph-freshness.md)). Install an agent protocol, local reader and checker, and read-only workflow through an explicit option ([ADR 0007](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/InternalOntology/blob/feature/source-knowledge-graph/architect/docs/adr/0007-source-graph-opt-in-runtime.md)). Use a versioned core RDF vocabulary with defined adopter extensions ([ADR 0008](https://github.com/jamiemitchellconsultants/InternalOntology/blob/feature/source-knowledge-graph/architect/docs/adr/0008-source-graph-vocabulary.md)).

## Consequences

A PR exposes changes to assertions, evidence, coverage, and no-fact-change reviews. The deterministic checker validates a documented canonical Turtle subset, structure, and freshness without making semantic claims; maintainers judge whether evidence supports direct or inferred assertions. The source graph can be combined with the canonical ontology by RDF consumers without translating JSON. Repositories can participate with partial coverage, and downstream consumers derive only the views their pinned facts support. The first implementation must define and test the Turtle contract, coverage priority, reader output, and local/CI revision modes. Numeric grounding targets remain deferred until a representative baseline exists.

## Entry 16 — 2026-11-02 — docs(feature): plan source knowledge graph implementation

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The accepted architecture fixes the behaviour of the graph but leaves several contract details to the developer: the shape of the graph settings in `OntologyConfig`, the IRIs for evidence roles and outcomes, how a deleted file is recorded, how a review record is named, and how the checker and reader are invoked locally and in CI. The plan has to settle these without changing a behaviour or an ADR, keep the installed scripts byte-identical across repositories, and let every claim be proved by a test that runs without a model, secret or network.

## Decision

Fill the gaps conservatively and record them in the task plan's decisions table. An evidence role with no configured selector accepts no evidence, so Terraform-only deployment is plain configuration. Every existing covered file must carry a review record whose blob equals its current blob; pull request mode adds the base-and-proposed union rule from ADR 0006 and a guard against a pull request disabling or relocating the check. Revisions are read from Git objects, including the index for a staged candidate, never from the working tree. Rejected: baking a fixed evidence default into the scripts, which would break byte-identical installs, and reading configuration from the working directory, which a pull request could rewrite.

## Consequences

The build can proceed task by task with each behaviour mapped to the task that proves it. The first broad declaration of coverage by an adopter needs one review record per covered file, which an agent must write by hand; the checker prints each expected blob ID, and a record-writing helper is left as a possible later change. The branch-protection integration of the new workflow is verified only in a disposable GitHub repository during the final task, or reported as unverified. Numeric grounding targets stay deferred.

## Entry 20 — 2026-11-03 — Plan final source graph review repairs

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Final review of the pushed build found that an empty evidence path with line zero produced no findings, graph opt-in beside an existing custom-namespace config wrote starter files in a different namespace, and removing a covered selector with its evidence and assertions escaped the PR check when source files did not change. The architecture requires removed coverage to remain explicitly unknown or excluded with a reason. GitHub branch-protection integration remains unverified.

## Decision

Compare each base covered selector by its literal pattern with proposed coverage declarations. Retain the selector as covered, or retain it as unknown or excluded with a non-empty reason; narrowing uses a reasoned old-scope marker plus a higher-priority covered selector for the retained area. Validate evidence paths and line bounds independently. Generate new starter graph files from a preserved config's namespace during normal opt-in or force; explicit reset replaces config and starters together. Append one Task 11 repair commit to the existing build branch without rewriting its ten task commits.

## Consequences

Coverage removal is visible even without changed source files. Literal pattern comparison avoids guessing glob equivalence from tracked files, so a selector rewrite must retain an explicit old-scope marker. The existing base/head review-record rule still applies to changed files. The installed checker, installer and acceptance tests receive focused regressions. The build handoff remains blocked until the plan amendment is reviewed and merged, the pushback is cleared, and Task 11 passes. Branch-protection integration remains for user acceptance.

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Final review found empty evidence paths and line zero could pass, starter graph files could use the wrong namespace beside an existing config, and a covered selector could disappear without a reasoned gap. The independent code review also reproduced malformed or unreferenced records passing when a changed file left coverage, because the head-only exemption skipped record validation.

## Decision

Validate evidence path syntax and line bounds independently. Compare base covered selectors by literal pattern with proposed declarations; retain a removed scope as reasoned unknown or excluded coverage. Use the preserved config's namespace for newly installed starter graph files, while explicit reset replaces config and starters together. Apply full review-record validation to changed paths covered by either the base or proposed graph, including paths that leave coverage in the proposed graph; continue ignoring old records for unchanged paths outside current coverage. Keep all repairs in the one Task 11 commit after the ten pushed task commits.

Graph-only scope removal is visible, and a transition PR cannot satisfy its remaining review obligation with a malformed record. Literal selector comparison avoids inferring glob equivalence from a finite file list, so a selector rewrite retains an explicit old-scope marker. Normal installation and force preserve adopter-owned config and graph data; reset discards them together. The checker still validates structure and review records, while maintainers judge semantic truth. GitHub branch-protection integration remains unverified for the user acceptance phase.

## Entry 34 — 2026-11-18 — docs: design configurable drift request budget (#100)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The drift reviewer's fixed 24,000-character budget makes it refuse to run for repositories with larger ontologies (JEPA-Speech, Grooveloom), failing with an unexplained red job. Scripts must stay byte-identical, so adopters cannot change the cap.

## Decision

Raise the default to 200,000 characters (about 50,000 to 67,000 tokens, at most half of a 131,072-token window), make the budget and the model timeout environment settings fed from repository variables with strict validation ([ADR 0014](docs/adr/0014-configurable-request-budget.md)), and turn an oversized ontology into a neutral skipped outcome: marker comment, notice, exit 0 ([ADR 0015](docs/adr/0015-skipped-outcome-for-oversized-ontology.md)). The 413 split stays the fallback. Rejected: config-file setting, deriving from a context-window setting, notice without a comment.

## Consequences

Large-ontology adopters work after a reinstall; larger requests cost more and the 300,000 ms timeout is unmeasured for them, so it is configurable and documented. Skipped runs leave a comment where clean runs stay silent. Splitting the ontology projection and changing `max_tokens` stay out of scope.

## Entry 38 — 2026-11-18 — docs: design configurable semantic reviewer request budget (#111)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The semantic reviewer plans requests against a fixed 24,000-character budget, so for ontologies as large as JEPA-Speech's (58,094 characters) or Grooveloom's (73,517) it never calls the model and publishes a success status reading "service or configuration unavailable", which blames the wrong thing and says nothing about the size. Feature #100 fixed only the advisory drift reviewer.

## Decision

Raise the default to 200,000 characters and make budget and timeout configurable with the #100 variables and validation, through one shared module ([ADR 0018](docs/adr/0018-shared-request-budget-module-and-timeout-default.md), which also raises the semantic request timeout default from 30,000 ms to 300,000 ms). A too-large ontology becomes its own non-blocking outcome ([ADR 0016](docs/adr/0016-too-large-ontology-outcome.md)). A junk setting publishes an explained unavailable run and then fails the job ([ADR 0017](docs/adr/0017-invalid-budget-setting-status.md)). Rejected: a failing status, a semantic-only variable name, keeping the 30,000 ms timeout.

## Consequences

Large-ontology adopters can review after a reinstall with `--force`. A hung model call can now hold a semantic request for up to five minutes. The 300,000 ms figure and the 200,000 default are unmeasured for the semantic reviewer on the live gateway. Splitting the projection and capping semantic output stay out of scope.

## Entry 41 — 2026-11-18 — fix: semantic reviewer reads fenced replies and resolves evidence keys

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

The first live trial of the blocking semantic reviewer showed that it never reviewed anything: the gateway's correct reply was fenced JSON with a singular section prefix in its evidence keys, and the reviewer rejected it as unusable without saying why.

Parse one surrounding code fence; resolve evidence keys to the unique catalog item with the same name instead of requiring an exact key; list the valid keys in the prompt; report fixed, specific reasons ([ADR 0019](docs/adr/0019-grounding-of-model-findings.md)). <a id="entry-docs-design-for-agent-maintained-knowledge-graph-122"></a>

## Entry 42 — 2026-11-18 — docs: design for agent-maintained knowledge graph (#122)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Agents in kit-installed repositories kept the ontology current but not the source graph. In JEPA-Speech, two features added ontology concepts and code outside the graph's coverage, and the graph only had its blob IDs refreshed. The accepted decision `docs-feature-behaviours-for-source-knowledge-graph` (#35 B11) kept semantic review of the graph human and ruled out model involvement. Settling an ontology semantic finding today needs `/ontology-dismiss` with a 64-hex finding ID and a 40-hex SHA, and the dismissal expires on every push.

## Decision

This is a correction of `docs-feature-behaviours-for-source-knowledge-graph`: a model may now produce semantic results about the graph, and a result takes effect only when a person with write access accepts it. The deterministic graph check stays model-free, secret-free and offline ([ADR 0020](docs/adr/0020-model-graph-naming-results-take-effect-on-human-acceptance.md)). #62 stands.

Agents look names up in the ontology and graph before naming code. They record symbols and components with `kit:implements` in the same change, propose the narrowest coverage widening for code in unknown scope, and follow authoring guidance kept in the installed runbook ([ADR 0025](docs/adr/0025-graph-authoring-guidance-in-the-installed-runbook.md)). A concept-first `GraphReader` command answers "what implements this concept?".

The naming review is a separate opt-in with its own workflows and status. It reuses the semantic review's environment, `ModelAuthProvider`, `RequestBudget` and `SemanticOutcome` ([ADR 0023](docs/adr/0023-graph-naming-review-as-a-separate-opt-in.md)). It compares only added or changed nodes, chosen deterministically, and drops any name that contains the canonical term before the model sees it ([ADR 0024](docs/adr/0024-deterministic-selection-and-prefilter-for-graph-naming.md)). Results appear in one summary comment edited in place, holding a bot-written ledger ([ADR 0022](docs/adr/0022-one-summary-comment-with-a-bot-ledger-for-graph-naming.md)). Anyone with write access settles them with `/graph-naming accept|reject|defer <R labels|all> [text]`. Settlements survive pushes, and a deferral creates one labelled issue ([ADR 0021](docs/adr/0021-settle-graph-naming-results-with-short-comment-commands.md)).

Rejected alternatives: model calls inside `GraphChecker`, results that block or pass on their own, checkboxes or review threads for settling, a new comment per run, extending the semantic review to cover Turtle, and a separate secret.

## Consequences

Unsettled or accepted results hold the merge. A rejection or deferral lets the PR proceed, and a run that cannot review never blocks. A write-role author can clear their own results, and the rule that agents never settle results relies on the protocol, because agents use the human's token. Adopters with semantic review already set up need no new secret. Some real mismatches are missed by design. Still open as follow-ups: a model check of whether evidence supports each claim, a sweep of the whole graph, and showing earlier settlements on later PRs. The generated narrative fragment for this PR must have its kind set to `correction` on the narrative automation PR, citing `docs-feature-behaviours-for-source-knowledge-graph`.

<a id="entry-docs-plan-agent-maintained-knowledge-graph-122"></a>

## Entry 43 — 2026-11-18 — docs: plan agent-maintained knowledge graph (#122)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The design pull request (#123) is merged with ADRs 0020–0025. The Architect's handoff left the developer to decide how to split the worker, what to reuse from the semantic reviewer, the prefilter's word rule, the ledger and command grammar edge cases, the acceptance approach, and the order of the plan.

## Decision

There are 13 test-first tasks. Tasks 1–3 are the agent half: the `GraphReader` `concept` command, the stronger `GraphAgentProtocol`, and "Authoring graph entries" in the installed runbook. They can be trialled in JEPA-Speech before the review half starts. Tasks 4–13 build the review half as six small modules: select, model, commands, github, ledger and worker, then the three workflows, the installer flag, an installed integration test and the docs.

- Reuse: the semantic modules only export `decodeBlob`, `stripFence` and `resolveEvidenceKey`, and `catalogOntology` gains a `rows` map, so the semantic reviewer behaves exactly as before. The naming review installs `semantic-review-github` and `semantic-review-model` without the rest of the semantic reviewer.
- Prefilter: words are PascalCase, acronym, lower-case or digit runs, compared case-insensitively. A label contains a name when the name's words appear in it in order and next to each other.
- Settlement: each command's targets are resolved once, when it is first seen or edited, and recorded in the ledger. So `all` never widens to results that appear later. Unknown labels are ignored, and labels whose result has gone are reported as no longer current.
- Bounds: at most 20 results per run, with stored text cut to 200 characters. The stored run keeps counts and at most 20 not-reviewed entries, so the summary comment stays under GitHub's limit.
- Acceptance: the integration test runs the installed scripts against a local model stand-in and the real GitHub client with an in-memory `fetch`.

Rejected: one large worker script, and a whole-graph naming sweep (deferred by U6).

## Consequences

The build cannot start until this plan is reviewed and merged. The existing `sourceGraph` deep-equal expectations in the config tests gain a `namingReview` default. Adopters who install `--with-graph-naming-review` without the semantic reviewer get two of its modules and their tests. Not verified: GitHub's `issue_comment` behaviour and the collaborator `role_name` values, which the user phase exercises in the deployed trial.

<a id="entry-fix-and-acceptance-agent-maintained-knowledge-graph-user-step-122"></a>

## Entry 45 — 2026-11-18 — fix and acceptance: agent-maintained knowledge graph user step (#122)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The user phase's acceptance tests found that an installed but not-opted-in naming review still posted a summary comment on every pull request. B34 and the installed runbook say only a disabled status is posted. The tests also found that the outcome was `partial` instead of `too-large` when the ontology exceeded the budget, so the status did not name the variable to raise. The pushback also claimed that an absent setting reported `unavailable`. That was wrong: `loadConfig` already turns an absent `sourceGraph.namingReview` into `enabled: false`.

## Decision

- A disabled run publishes only the status, on head and merge, and posts no comment. A run that cannot read the trusted configuration at all stays `unavailable`.
- When every name bound for the model was too large for the budget and no model call succeeded, the outcome is `too-large`. Names settled without the model, because they contain their canonical term or are of a skipped kind, no longer make it `partial`.
- The review half is accepted locally through executable tests only. A walkthrough run by hand would need GitHub, so those behaviours are walked through in the JEPA-Speech trial.

## Consequences

Repositories that install `--with-graph-naming-review` and never opt in see no comments from it. If a repository disables the review partway through a pull request, the summary comment from the earlier enabled run stays as it was, while the status turns to a disabled success. The runbook's Outcomes table now matches what a run reports. The deployed acceptance in JEPA-Speech, and the JEPA-Speech reinstall it needs, wait for this merge.

<a id="entry-docs-design-for-matched-ontology-projection-135"></a>

## Entry 46 — 2026-11-19 — docs: design for matched ontology projection (#135)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Every semantic review request resent the whole ontology projection: 64,394 characters for JEPA-Speech's 202 entries. A growing ontology runs into the `RequestBudget` and is reported as `too-large`. Raising `ONTOLOGY_MAX_REQUEST_CHARS` only moves that limit, every resend costs time and tokens, and the model has to find the relevant rows among hundreds. All ten recorded findings were paraphrases, such as "AuditRecord" for an entity named differently, so matching exact names would have missed every one of them.

## Decision

The semantic reviewer now sends, by default, only the entries deterministically matched to the Markdown. An entry matches through its exact name, a banned alias, or the words of its name or enum values, and each match adds one hop of references. Every request also carries the name index of every entry, and `semanticReview.projection: "full"` restores today's request byte for byte.

The selection lives in a new `ontology-projection.mjs` that the worker injects into `reviewFiles`, so the graph naming reviewer is untouched ([ADR 0026](docs/adr/0026-matched-projection-as-an-injected-projector.md)). The matching rule and a fixed stop list of generic modelling words are in [ADR 0027](docs/adr/0027-deterministic-matching-rule-and-fixed-stop-list.md). The setting is validated for `semanticReview` only, and the per-file projection summary is an optional field in the run record, which stays at schema 1 ([ADR 0028](docs/adr/0028-projection-setting-and-run-record-summary.md)).

Rejected alternatives:
- matching exact names only, which found none of the ten;
- matching rare words only, which found four;
- relationship rows only for "related";
- a configurable stop list;
- embedding retrieval, which is deferred to a later feature.

## Consequences

Adopters get smaller requests after reinstalling with `--force`, but the saving is modest, mostly because of the one hop. A paraphrase that shares no name word with its entry is reviewed against the name index only. The pull request record now shows, for each reviewed file, what it was checked against. Setting `"full"` before updating the kit gives an invalid-config run. The stop list is fixed, so changing it needs a kit release. Embedding retrieval can later replace the projector without reshaping the reviewer.

<a id="entry-docs-implementation-plans-for-matched-ontology-projection-135"></a>

## Entry 47 — 2026-11-19 — docs: implementation plans for matched ontology projection (#135)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The design for #135 (PR #136, ADRs 0026–0028) settled what a matched `OntologyProjection` contains and how the reviewer uses it. The plan step had to turn that into tasks without re-deciding anything. Two things the design assumed did not hold exactly:
- **B17's subset claim.** The design assumed a chunk never selects more ontology than its whole file. A chunk cut inside an oversized line can create a word or a whole-name match the file lacks, so its own projection can be larger than the one the plan was budgeted against.
- **The default changes an existing test.** Making `matched` the default changes what an existing #111 acceptance test exercises. That test relied on the full projection of a 60 KB ontology not fitting 24,000 characters, but the name index alone fits.

## Decision

- **Guard against over-budget chunks.** `reviewFiles` checks each request's size after projecting its chunk. A chunk that would exceed the `RequestBudget` is split before it is sent, exactly as on a 413. At one character it is reported `too-large` with the budget reason. Nothing over budget is ever sent, and the projector interface stays as ADR 0026 defines it.
- **Pin the #111 test to `"full"`.** That test now sets `projection: "full"`, so it keeps proving the full projection's too-large path. The new acceptance test covers the matched one (a budget below the name index).
- **Keep the model module's tests independent of the projector.** `semantic-review-model.mjs` and its test use stub projectors and never import the projection module, because graph-naming-only installs copy them without it.
- **Reject `null` explicitly.** `semanticReview.projection` defaults only when the key is absent. An explicit `null` is rejected like any other value.

## Consequences

- The build can proceed from the detailed plan without design questions. A smaller model can run it task by task, because every test it needs is written out and has already been run.
- The guard adds one size check per request and changes nothing when a chunk's projection fits, which is every case in `full` mode.
- The #111 acceptance suite now names its mode explicitly. A later change to the default does not silently change what it tests.

<a id="entry-feat-matched-ontology-projection-for-the-semantic-reviewer-135"></a>

## Entry 48 — 2026-11-19 — feat: matched ontology projection for the semantic reviewer (#135)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The semantic reviewer sent the whole ontology projection with every request. The kit is to be rolled out to repositories with much larger ontologies, where the whole projection would no longer fit the request budget and every review would be too large. Today's repositories are small enough that the difference is slight.

## Decision

Each request carries a deterministic matched projection by default: the full rows of the entries its chunk selects, plus the name index, so the model can still cite any entry and every citation is checked against the whole catalog ([ADR 0026](docs/adr/0026-matched-projection-as-an-injected-projector.md), [ADR 0027](docs/adr/0027-deterministic-matching-rule-and-fixed-stop-list.md)). `"full"` restores the old request byte for byte, and the record shows each file's projection ([ADR 0028](docs/adr/0028-projection-setting-and-run-record-summary.md)). Rejected for now: embedding-based retrieval, which is deferred to a later feature.

## Consequences

Request size now grows with the entries a chunk selects rather than with the whole ontology, so larger ontologies stay reviewable. A matched review can miss a paraphrase that shares no name word with its entry; repositories that care more about that than about request size can set `"full"`. The stop list is fixed in the script for every adopter, so changing it changes every repository's requests.

<a id="entry-matched-ontology-projection-design-amendment-after-acceptance-pushback-1"></a>

## Entry 49 — 2026-11-20 — Matched ontology projection: design amendment after acceptance pushback (#135)

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

User acceptance of #135 passed every behaviour as written, but showed that the matched `OntologyProjection` would not keep large ontologies inside the `RequestBudget`, which is the reason the feature exists. Measured with the shipped projector:
- **Broad files.** Planning a file against the projection of its whole text made a broad file too-large in matched mode, exactly as in full. In a 1,920-entry synthetic ontology, a 3.4 KB file naming one entry per context projected 330,898 of 331,071 characters, although each paragraph projected about 74,500. JEPA-Speech's graph README already projects 63% of its full projection, and six of the ten recorded findings came from it.
- **The one hop.** It accounted for most of each request on real ontologies: the median matched request was 79% of the full projection on JEPA-Speech, and 52% with relationships only.
- **The name index.** At about 30 characters per entry, it alone filled the 200,000-character default at about 6,700 entries.

Separately, `ontology.ttl` is the source of truth and `ontology.md` is generated from it, but the reviewer read only the generated file.

## Decision

- **Plan by paragraph ([ADR 0030](docs/adr/0030-matched-planning-by-paragraph-in-the-projector.md)).**
  - The matched projector gains a `plan` step. It indexes the catalog once, selects for each paragraph once, and packs paragraphs, then lines, then pieces of a line, while each request fits with its own projection.
  - `full` mode keeps today's planner, so it stays byte for byte.
  - The two too-large causes, the name index or a line that selects too much, get their own reasons.
  - Rejected: packing in the model module, re-projecting the whole candidate text for every paragraph, planning against the largest paragraph's projection, and a fixed chunk size.
- **Relationships only, and a grouped name index ([ADR 0031](docs/adr/0031-relationships-only-and-grouped-name-index.md)).**
  - A matched entry adds the relationships whose domain or range it is, and nothing else.
  - In matched mode the name index lists the names under each section, introduced by one explanatory sentence. The system prompt is unchanged.
  - Rejected: keeping the hop, adding far-end entries, no hop at all, keeping one key per line, and indexing only nearby entries.
- **Read the ontology source ([ADR 0029](docs/adr/0029-semantic-review-reads-the-ontology-source.md)).**
  - The reviewer reads `ontology.ttl` at the reviewed revision and renders it exactly as `build-ontology.mjs` does, so evidence keys, rows and finding identities are unchanged.
  - It falls back to `ontology.md` when the source is absent, as on a fresh install before its first build.
  - Rejected: selecting from the triples directly, and making the run unavailable without a `.ttl`.
- **Deferred with measurements:** limiting name words that many entries share, and matching alternative labels.

## Consequences

- **Broad files.** A file whose paragraphs each fit is always reviewed. Matched requests on JEPA-Speech should shrink from a median of 79% to about 52% of the full projection, and all ten recorded findings are kept.
- **Ontology ceiling.** The grouped index is 40% to 49% smaller, which lifts the ceiling at the default budget to about 10,000 to 11,500 entries. Above that, raising `ONTOLOGY_MAX_REQUEST_CHARS` remains the remedy.
- **Live check needed.** The model must now form `Section:Name` from the grouped index. `resolveEvidenceKey` tolerates a bare name, but acceptance must include a live model run.
- **Paraphrase caveat.** A paraphrase caught only through a neighbouring entry's rows is no longer caught. The runbook caveat must say so.
- **Fallback.** A repository whose `ontology.md` is stale is reviewed against its `ontology.ttl`. One without a `.ttl` keeps today's behaviour.
- **Later phases to regenerate:** the plan, the build, the runbook, and the acceptance tests (b1a2a41 on `feature/matched-ontology-projection/user`). Once this merges, run `node scripts/feature.mjs clear-pushback --feature 135 --phase analyst`.

<a id="entry-docs-define-semantic-repository-index-vision"></a>

## Entry 50 — 2026-11-20 — docs: define semantic repository index vision

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Developers and coding agents often know the behaviour they need to find before they know the exact names used in an unfamiliar repository. The Ontology Kit already gives them canonical vocabulary and optional source graph evidence. Code Context and Greptile demonstrate semantic retrieval and cross-file context. Adopting repositories need control over the embedding model and a way to share precomputed vectors with teammates.

## Decision

Offer semantic repository search as an opt-in capability. The repository owner supplies the embedding model and approves the indexed content. Each checkout uses a rebuildable, Git-ignored vector store. Developers with repository access can download a snapshot from the adopting repository's GitHub Releases, and a publisher with write access can upload a snapshot for a pushed commit.

## Consequences

A developer can reuse the published vectors with access to the matching model and refresh the local index as source changes. Release assets keep generated vectors out of Git history and give the snapshot a repository-owned distribution point. The pilot will compare search quality with keyword search and measure refresh work and asset size. Snapshot selection, publication cadence, and implementation choices carry forward to later phases.
